You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (mean in 0.7-0.8s).
        *   $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (absolute max).
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (ripple in 0.7-0.8s).
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (time to reach 1.8V).
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (stability between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s).
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{M}\Omega$ leakage.
    *   Operating Conditions (S1-S6): Varying $I_p, f, C_p, R_L$, and temperature.
    *   Reference Design (FBR) failed on several counts:
        *   S3: $V_{max}$ too high (overvoltage).
        *   S4: $V_{avg}$ too low, $t_{up}$ too slow.
        *   S5: $V_{avg}$ too low.
        *   S6: $V_{avg}$ too low.
        *   S2: Ripple too high, $t_{up}$ too slow.

    *   Piezo output is AC. The open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$ (S1).
    *   FBR is simple but suffers from:
        *   Diode drops (reducing $V_{avg}$ for low $I_p$ or heavy load).
        *   Lack of voltage regulation (S3 exceeds 3.6V).
        *   Inefficient energy transfer (no impedance matching).
    *   To improve:
        *   **Overvoltage Protection**: A Zener diode (DZ33) can clamp the output to 3.3V.
        *   **Efficiency/Voltage Boost**: Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) or similar techniques.
        *   **Low-drop Rectification**: Use DSCH (Schottky) or SYNC switches to reduce losses.

    *   **Design 1: FBR + Zener Clamp**. This addresses the S3 $V_{max}$ failure.
    *   **Design 2: SSHI (Parallel-SSHI)**. This increases the harvested energy by inverting the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the voltage across the rectifier.
    *   **Design 3: Half-Bridge Rectifier with Zener**. Since pzn is often effectively ground in some configurations, or to reduce diode drops. But FBR is generally better for AC current sources. Let's try a **Synchronous Rectifier (Active Bridge)** or a **Boost-like structure**. Actually, a simpler "Buck-Boost" or "Inductive-Boost" using SYNC might be too complex. Let's go with a "Standard SSHI" (Parallel) first.

    *   **Top 1: FBR + Zener (The "Safe" Baseline)**
        *   Components: 4x DSCH (FBR), 1x DZ33 (Clamp), 1x C (Storage).
        *   Rationale: Solves $V_{max}$ failure of S3.

    *   **Top 2: P-SSHI (Parallel SSHI)**
        *   Components: L, S (SYNC), 4x DSCH (Rectifier), 1x C (Storage), 1x DZ33 (Clamp).

            1.  Inductor $L$ connected between `pzp` and a switch $S$.

            3.  Rectifier from `pzp` (or `pzn`) to `out`.
            *Actually, a simpler P-SSHI:* $L$ is in parallel with the piezo, flipped by a switch at the peaks.
            *Correct SSHI Topology (Simplified):*
            - $L$ from `pzp` to `n1`.
            - $S$ from `n1` to `pzn`.
            - $S$ is controlled by SYNC.
            - Rectifier (FBR) from `pzp` and `pzn` to `out`.
            - $C$ at `out`.
            - $DZ33$ clamp at `out`.

    *   **Top 3: Synchronous Rectifier (Active Bridge)**
        *   Using SYNC switches instead of diodes.
        *   S1: `pzp` to `out` (controlled by SYNC G1, edges="pos")
        *   S2: `pzn` to `out` (controlled by SYNC G2, edges="neg")
        *   S3: `out` to `pzp` (G1) - wait, that's not how it works.

    *   $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$.
    *   The load $R_L$ can be as low as $150\text{k}\Omega$.

    *   The main issues are $V_{max}$ on S3 ($R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$) and $V_{avg}$ on S4, S5, S6.

    *   P-SSHI increases the available voltage.
    *   Topology:
        *   $L1$: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
        *   $S1$: `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (Ctrl: $G1$, edges="both", ton $\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$)

Actually, a **Full Bridge with DZ33** and an **L-S (SSHI) circuit** is the strongest candidate.
        *   Let's refine Proposal 3: **SSHI with a larger output capacitor** (handled by evolution) and **Tuning Inductor** for resonance.

    *Wait*, I can propose 3 different structures.
    1. `FBR_Zener`: FBR + DZ33. (Low risk, fixes S3)
    2. `PSSHI_Zener`: P-SSHI + FBR + DZ33. (High reward, fixes S4, S5, S6)
    3. `Active_HalfBridge`: Using SYNC switches instead of diodes to reduce drop.
       - S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (G1, "pos")
       - S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (G2, "neg")
       - (This is a half-bridge; it only harvests half the cycle).
       Let's try a **Synchronous Full-Bridge** (if it fits in 16 components and 4 switches).
       - S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (G1, "pos")
       - S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (G2, "neg")
       - S3: `0` $\to$ `pzp` (G2, "neg") - No, that's not right.
       - S4: `0` $\to$ `pzn` (G1, "pos")
       Actually, a full synchronous bridge needs 4 switches. Let's try:
       - S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (G1, "pos")
       - S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (G2, "neg")
       - S3: `out` $\to$ `pzp` - No.

    *Let's go with these 3:*
    1. `FBR_Zener`
    2. `PSSHI_Zener`
    3. `S_HalfBridge_Zener` (S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`, S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` using SYNC, + DZ33).

    *Self-Correction on P-SSHI:*
    $L$ is from `pzp` to `n1`. $S$ is from `n1` to `pzn`. $S$ closes at the peaks of $V_{pzp}$.
    $V_{pzp}$ peaks when $I_{piezo} = 0$. This is exactly what SYNC does ("edges": "both").
    The rectifier (FBR) is then connected to the piezo.

    *Components check for PSSHI_Zener:*
    - L1: `pzp`, `n1`
    - S1: `n1`, `pzn` (G1)
    - G1: SYNC
    - D1: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
    - D2: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
    - D3: `0`, `pzp` (DSCH)
    - D4: `0`, `pzn` (DSCH)
    - D5: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
    - C1: `out`, `0`
    Total: 9 components. Well within 16.

    *Refining S_HalfBridge_Zener (Proposal 3):*
    Wait, a half-bridge rectifier using switches:
    - S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (G1, "pos")
    - S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (G2, "neg")
    - C1: `out`, `0`
    - D1: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
    This only works if `pzn` is grounded. If `pzn` isn't grounded, it's just a current source. We need a return path to 0.
    So, a full bridge is better. Let's replace Proposal 3 with a **Synchronous Full Bridge (4 switches)**.
    - S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (G1, "pos")
    - S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (G2, "neg")
    - S3: `0` $\to$ `pzn` (G1, "pos")
    - S4: `0` $\to$ `pzp` (G2, "neg")
    - C1: `out`, `0`
    - D1: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
    - G1: SYNC ("pos")
    - G2: SYNC ("neg")
    Total: 9 components.

    *Checking the SYNC logic for the full bridge:*
    - At positive peak of $V_{pzp}$: $S1$ (`pzp` $\to$ `out`) and $S3$ (`0` $\to$ `pzn`) close. Current flows $0 \to pzn \to pzp \to out$.
    - At negative peak of $V_{pzp}$: $S2$ (`pzn` $\to$ `out`) and $S4$ (`0` $\to$ `pzp`) close. Current flows $0 \to pzp \to pzn \to out$.
    This is a synchronous rectifier. It should have almost zero drop.

    1. `FBR_Zener`: Baseline + Clamp.
    2. `PSSHI_Zener`: SSHI + FBR + Clamp. (Best for voltage boost)
    3. `SyncBridge_Zener`: Synchronous Bridge + Clamp. (Best for efficiency/drop)

    *One last check on SSHI:* The SYNC `ton` is crucial. The evolution strategy will optimize it. The `phase` might also be adjusted.

    *L-Cp Inversion in SSHI:*
    $L$ is in series with the switch $S$. When $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ form a resonant circuit. The charge on $C_p$ is flipped. This increases the voltage seen by the rectifier.

    *Double-check components:*
    `FBR_Zener`:
    - D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
    - D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
    - D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
    - D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
    - D5: 0, out (DZ33)
    - C1: out, 0

    `PSSHI_Zener`:
    - L1: pzp, n1
    - S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    - G1: SYNC (edges: "both")
    - D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
    - D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
    - D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
    - D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
    - D5: 0, out (DZ33)
    - C1: out, 0

    `SyncBridge_Zener`:
    - S1: pzp, out (ctrl: G1)
    - S2: pzn, out (ctrl: G2)
    - S3: 0, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    - S4: 0, pzp (ctrl: G2)
    - G1: SYNC (edges: "pos")
    - G2: SYNC (edges: "neg")
    - D1: 0, out (DZ33)
    - C1: out, 0

    Wait, in `SyncBridge_Zener`, G1 and G2 are two separate controllers. This is allowed (at most 2).
    Wait, the `S3` and `S4` switches:
    - G1 closes S1 and S3. (pos peak)
    - G2 closes S2 and S4. (neg peak)
    This effectively creates a low-resistance path during the peak.

    Wait, a detail: The piezo is a *current source* $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$.
    The voltage $V_{pzp}$ is the integral of the current.
    The current is zero at the voltage peaks.
    SYNC closes switches at the "piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current".
    This is perfect for SSHI and Synchronous Rectification.

    - All 3 use a Zener `DZ33` to protect against $V_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$ (S3).
    - `FBR_Zener` is a simple safety check.
    - `PSSHI_Zener` uses an inductor to boost voltage, addressing $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$ (S4, S5, S6).
    - `SyncBridge_Zener` removes diode drops, addressing $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$ (S4, S5, S6).

    Check component counts:
    - `FBR_Zener`: 6
    - `PSSHI_Zener`: 9
    - `SyncBridge_Zener`: 8
    All under 16.
